newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand launches proposed pension saving scheme.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand launches proposed pension saving scheme.

text.p: New Zealand on Monday launched its long-awaited and controversial contributory pension scheme which, if introduced, would require all earners who can to save up to NZ$120,000 ($81,000) towards the cost of their own pension.

A government white paper published during the day said that if a referendum due in September endorses the Retirement Savings Scheme (RSS), everyone earning over NZ$96 a week will have to contribute 3 percent of their incomes from next July.
The exact level of the compulsory annuity savers have to aim for will be set after consultation with the fund management industry which is expected to run qualifying schemes, it added.

Employees' required contribution level will rise over the five years following RSS' introduction to 8.0 percent, provided the government can afford tax cuts it has promised will be brought in to offset the increases in contributions.
An 86-page government document, which has been half a year in the making, said the tax cuts would be guaranteed in the first year, but then would only happen "when fiscally sustainable".

Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters said the time was right for RSS, which has largely been his own political crusade since he promised in last year's election campaign that he would let the public decide if they wanted to change.
"(It) solves the problem of future affordability posed by the impending retirement of the baby boom generation," he told a briefing that included representatives of the pension industry.
New Zealand's 3.72 million population, like those of many other developed nations, surged after the end of World War II but its rate of growth has since slowed.
This means that, almost a century after it launched a pioneering universal state pension scheme, New Zealand now believes it will struggle to support ever-higher payouts.

"Next century it will be harder to provide an adequate retirement income from taxation. As a greater percentage of the population retires, the ratio of workers to retired people will grow smaller and smaller," Peters said.
However, his political opponents took issue with some of his assumptions, and some defended the existing universal superannuation scheme saying it could be sustained.

Opposition Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen said that his party's approach was to adapt the existing scheme with a "tax and fund regime" rather than taking what he called "an unnecessary gamble" that relied on future tax cuts.
According to the White Paper, RSS' target is to ensure every person has saved enough for an annuity equivalent to 33 percent of the average after-tax wage when they reach 65.

Under a plan intended to avoid any distortion between men and women's contributions, because women live longer, the paper proposes giving women extra funds so they can match the standard men's annuity level without having to pay more.
Anyone who cannot save the required amount will receive a lump-sum top-up from the government, and noone over 60 will be expected to contribute to the scheme at all.
The first generation due to contribute the entire $120,000 would be people born since April 1, 1973.
Although a full public information campaign is due to start at the end of July, a pamphlet summarising the white paper is to be distributed to all households on Tuesday, Peters said.
Polls show most New Zealanders oppose Peters' proposal.
A poll of 933 people last week by financial services group Colonial showed opposition to the scheme had risen to 63 percent from 59 percent in May.
